item.title: SeatGeek Canada hit with more fines totalling $22,500 over ticket resale violations
item.description: SeatGeek Canada is facing two more fines from the Ontario government for allegedly contravening a recent law capping the sale of event tickets at face value.
item.dc:creator: The Canadian Press
item.content:encoded: TORONTO — SeatGeek Canada is facing two more fines from the Ontario government for allegedly contravening a recent law capping the sale of event tickets at face value. The province’s consumer beware website shows the new fines issued to the ticket resale platform earlier this month total $22,500 collectively. The website says the first of the two fines amounts to $15,000 and is for allegedly making a ticket available for sale or facilitating a sale of a seat beyond the resale price limit. The second fine is for $7,500 and is for allegedly failing to disclose the total price of a ticket when a seat was purchased from a primary seller. SeatGeek Canada did not immediately respond to questions about what events the fines stem from or whether it will fight the penalties. Giulia Paikin, a spokesperson for the Ontario Minister of Public and Business Service Delivery Stephen Crawford, also did not answer questions about the nature of the penalties. However, she sent a statement that repeated nearly verbatim what the province has previously said about anyone responsible for price cap violations facing fines of up to $250,000.  “We will not hesitate to hold bad actors who break the rules accountable,” an email from Paikin said. SeatGeek’s new fines stem from legislation the province implemented earlier this year, after fans complained about resale prices for tickets to Taylor Swift’s Eras tour in 2024 and last year’s playoff run by the Toronto Blue Jays. The legislation was meant to keep people from reselling seats to Ontario events for well beyond face value and tamp down on scalpers profiting off their ability to scoop up tickets to hot concerts and shows. After the legislation came into effect, the province issued $25,000 in fines to SeatGeek in August for similar offences. A $20,000 fine for fellow resale website StubHub Canada followed in September. When SeatGeek was given its first round of fines, it told The Canadian Press it had notified third-party sellers on its platform about the new law but was still seeking guidance from the province around how to comply with the regulations. The platform argued it is challenging to confirm the original value of tickets because many sellers don’t have access to that information. Sometimes seats have changed hands several times before they wind up on a resale site and if tickets were bought as part of a broader package, like a season’s seat arrangement, it can be hard to break down the value of a single ticket. To address these issues, SeatGeek said it has asked Ontario to define what counts as acceptable proof of a ticket’s original price and for guidance around how a marketplace is expected to validate the cost of seats. --- Tara Deschamps, The Canadian Press This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 15, 2026.

item.title: CNN, Axios and other publishers join Google’s AI news program
item.description: Skydance’s, the Financial Times, Axios and other publishers joined Google’s news program to license their content for generative AI features.
item.dc:creator: Reuters Staff
item.content:encoded: Skydance’s, the Financial Times, Axios and other publishers joined Google’s news program to license their content for generative AI features and explore ways to drive audience engagement. The search-engine giant said on Thursday that the program, which started as a pilot last year with partners like The Washington Post, now includes more than 400 publications globally. The deal marks CNN’s first partnership since Paramount Skydance completed its acquisition of Warner Bros Discovery, as CEO David Ellison seeks to position the combined company as a technology-driven media business. As part of these agreements, publishers will provide enhanced content rights, allowing Google to develop new AI features, while Google will pay participating news organizations for their content. Financial terms were not disclosed. “Google’s innovation with generative AI has changed how people discover information and content, and now those tools will help us explore new ways to discover and engage audiences,” said Sam Felix, CNN’s senior vice president of strategic partnerships and business development. Google said the AI features will come with clear attribution and direct links, helping readers to connect with the sources they value. The announcement comes at a time when publishers are stepping up legal efforts to prevent AI companies from using their content without permission to train large language models. News publishers are also grappling with declining referral traffic as search engines roll out AI-generated answers that allow users to consume information without clicking through to websites. CNN said the deal is in line with its strategy to protect its intellectual property, adding that it has multiple commercial partnerships and ongoing discussions with other industry players. The network operates television, streaming and digital news services worldwide, including CNN International and CNN Originals, as well as a direct-to-consumer subscription service and CNN Newsource. --- Reporting by Harshita Mary Varghese and Jaspreet Singh in Bengaluru; Editing by Vijay Kishore and Anil D’Silva

item.title: Canada’s farmers and crop quality assessors confront damage after wet harvest
item.description: Canada’s farmers struggled to harvest this year’s crops due to an unseasonably wet September, and farmers and crop quality assessors reported damage to pulse crops and spring wheat in one of the world ...
item.dc:creator: Reuters Staff
item.content:encoded: WINNIPEG -- Canada’s farmers struggled to harvest this year’s crops due to an unseasonably wet September, and farmers and crop quality assessors reported damage to pulse crops and spring wheat in one of the world’s top-five world wheat exporters. Farmers were weeks behind their usual harvesting progress in many Prairie provinces from the beginning of September through early October, normally the driest time of the growing season. For example, by September 21, Saskatchewan’s harvest was 41 per cent done, compared to the five year average of 82 per cent. Most farmers have since completed harvesting, but the crop many brought in was degraded from the top quality prospect they had at the end of August. Lack of quality crops from Canada could contribute to tighter global wheat stocks and broadly higher food prices amid wars in Ukraine and the Middle East. Manitoba farmer Eric McLean had what he thought were great wheat and oats crops in his fields in August, but now a few of them are write-offs, he thinks. “There’s an adjuster coming here within the hour,” said McLean. Crop insurance will cover some of his losses, he hopes. Fields he managed to harvest in early September between rains produced good crops, but those left out suffered. Canada is the world’s biggest exporter of durum wheat used in pasta, of canola, used as vegetable oil, and for pulse crops like lentils, which are mainstay food crops in India and the Middle East. Its spring wheat crop is valued by global bread-makers. Canola is less impacted by rain damage due to its hard shell. Official government and industry estimates reflecting the damage won’t come until mid-November. But Reuters visited the Canadian Grain Commission’s headquarters in Winnipeg and found inspectors poring through examples of spring wheat that had suffered sprouting, likely making that crop unworthy of a food grade, and of red lentils that had been bleached and suffered shriveling from the September rains. Saskatchewan, the top wheat growing province, saw over three times normal precipitation in its main growing areas, leaving farmers struggling to find any days on which it was dry enough to harvest crops. The late rains add to the challenges some crops had with early summer rainfall, which caused fungal disease outbreaks. “We’ve had some very heavy late-season rainfall,” said agricultural weather expert Eric Snodgrass, a senior science fellow with Nutrien Ag Solutions, which advises farmers on crop production. Saskatchewan farmer Cory Loessin was relieved to have just finished harvesting on Oct. 7. He’s now spending on propane to dry down the wet wheat he harvested, which he normally doesn’t have to do. “We’re drying 90 per cent of the wheat crop we harvested,” said Loessin. Usually it’s about 10 per cent. (Reporting by Ed White; Editing by Caroline Stauffer and Nick Zieminski)
